\chapter{Este --- Pointing at What Is in Your Hand}
\label{ch:este}
\hlchaptermodality{221}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something next to me.}

I can point at something next to me.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[este]{este — pointing at what is in your hand}

\label{lesson:ES-C59-este}



\begin{quote}
\emph{El libro} names a book. But which one?

If it is in your hand, you need a word that \textbf{points}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{este libro} — \emph{this book}, the one right here.

It agrees like any other word that leans on a noun:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{\textbf{este}} \emph{libro} & this book \\
\emph{\textbf{esta}} \emph{casa} & this house \\
\emph{\textbf{estos}} \emph{libros} & these books \\
\emph{\textbf{estas}} \emph{casas} & these houses \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Latin's word was \emph{\textbf{iste}}, and it did not mean \emph{this}. It meant \textbf{that of yours} — it pointed at the person being spoken to. Spanish walked it one step closer, off the listener and onto the speaker's own hand, and it has stayed there ever since.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Now the part English speakers get wrong, and it is a rule rather than a habit.

\begin{quote}
\emph{este libro} — never \emph{el este libro}.
\end{quote}

The pointing word goes \textbf{in front} of the noun, and it takes the article's place. It does not stand beside it. You cannot have both, because both are doing the same job — saying \emph{which one} — and Spanish only lets one word do that job at a time.

So the moment you reach for \emph{este}, the \emph{el} you were about to say is already spoken for.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{este libro}, \emph{esta casa}
  \item \emph{estos libros}, \emph{estas casas}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{este} stand, and what does it push out? (\textbf{Before} the noun, in the \emph{\textbf{article's}} place.)

And who did Latin's \emph{iste} originally point at? (\textbf{You} — the person being spoken to. Spanish moved it closer.)
\end{tcolorbox}
